claim: Ciliary motility is driven by axonemal dyneins that are assembled in the cytoplasm before deployment to cilia.
source: Ciliary motility is driven by axonemal dyneins that are assembled in the cytoplasm before deployment to cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about ciliary biology.

claim: Motile ciliopathy can result from defects in the dyneins themselves or from defects in factors required for their cytoplasmic pre-assembly.
source: Motile ciliopathy can result from defects in the dyneins themselves or from defects in factors required for their cytoplasmic pre-assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about motile ciliopathy.

claim: Axonemal dyneins, their specific assembly factors, and broadly-acting chaperones are concentrated in liquid-like organelles in the cytoplasm called DynAPs (Dynein Axonemal Particles).
source: Recent work demonstrates that axonemal dyneins, their specific assembly factors, and broadly-acting chaperones are concentrated in liquid-like organelles in the cytoplasm called DynAPs (Dynein Axonemal Particles).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as recent work, referencing prior findings.

claim: Inner dynein arm (IDA) and outer dynein arm (ODA) subunits are partitioned into non-overlapping sub-regions within DynAPs.
source: Here, we use in vivo imaging in Xenopus to show that inner dynein arm (IDA) and outer dynein arm (ODA) subunits are partitioned into non-overlapping sub-regions within DynAPs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: C16orf71/Daap1 is a novel axonemal dynein regulator.
source: Among these, we identify C16orf71/Daap1 as a novel axonemal dynein regulator.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by APMS data and functional experiments.

claim: Daap1 interacts with ODA subunits.
source: Daap1 interacts with ODA subunits, localizes specifically to the cytoplasm, is enriched in DynAPs, and is required for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by APMS data in Figure 5A.

claim: Daap1 localizes specifically to the cytoplasm.
source: Daap1 interacts with ODA subunits, localizes specifically to the cytoplasm, is enriched in DynAPs, and is required for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Daap1 is enriched in DynAPs.
source: Daap1 interacts with ODA subunits, localizes specifically to the cytoplasm, is enriched in DynAPs, and is required for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Daap1 is required for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes.
source: Daap1 interacts with ODA subunits, localizes specifically to the cytoplasm, is enriched in DynAPs, and is required for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by knockdown experiments in Figure 9.

claim: Motile cilia are microtubule-based cellular projections.
source: Motile cilia are microtubule-based cellular projections and their oriented beating generates fluid flows that are critical for development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about motile cilia.

claim: Oriented beating of motile cilia generates fluid flows that are critical for development and homeostasis.
source: Motile cilia are microtubule-based cellular projections and their oriented beating generates fluid flows that are critical for development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about motile cilia function.

claim: Ciliary beating is driven by a complex set of axoneme-specific dynein motors that drive sliding of the axonemal microtubule doublets.
source: Ciliary beating is driven by a complex set of axoneme-specific dynein motors that drive sliding of the axonemal microtubule doublets.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about ciliary beating mechanism.

claim: Axonemal dynein motors are classified as either outer dynein arms (ODAs) or inner dynein arms (IDAs) based on their relative positions within the axoneme.
source: Based on their relative positions within the axoneme, these motors are classified as either outer dynein arms (ODAs) or inner dynein arms (IDAs)(Figure 1A, upper inset), the former driving ciliary beating generally, and the latter tuning the waveform (Kamiya and Yagi, 2014; King, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ODAs drive ciliary beating generally.
source: Based on their relative positions within the axoneme, these motors are classified as either outer dynein arms (ODAs) or inner dynein arms (IDAs)(Figure 1A, upper inset), the former driving ciliary beating generally, and the latter tuning the waveform (Kamiya and Yagi, 2014; King, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Kamiya and Yagi, 2014; King, 2018.

claim: IDAs tune the ciliary beating waveform.
source: Based on their relative positions within the axoneme, these motors are classified as either outer dynein arms (ODAs) or inner dynein arms (IDAs)(Figure 1A, upper inset), the former driving ciliary beating generally, and the latter tuning the waveform (Kamiya and Yagi, 2014; King, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Kamiya and Yagi, 2014; King, 2018.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding ODA or IDA subunits are the major cause of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD).
source: Mutations in genes encoding ODA or IDA subunits are the major cause of the motile ciliopathy syndrome known as primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD; MIM 244400).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about PCD genetics.

claim: PCD results in repeated sinopulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, cardiac defects, situs anomalies, and infertility.
source: This genetic disease results in repeated sinopulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, cardiac defects, situs anomalies, and infertility (Horani et al., 2016; Mitchison and Valente, 2017; Wallmeier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Horani et al., 2016; Mitchison and Valente, 2017; Wallmeier et al., 2020.

claim: PCD can result from mutations in genes encoding cytoplasmic proteins known as Dynein Axonemal Assembly Factors (DNAAFs).
source: Interestingly, PCD can also result from mutations in genes encoding any of several cytoplasmic proteins collectively known as Dynein Axonemal Assembly Factors (DNAAFs)(Desai et al., 2018; Fabczak and Osinka, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Desai et al., 2018; Fabczak and Osinka, 2019.

claim: Axonemal dynein motors were known to be pre-assembled in the cytoplasm before deployment to cilia.
source: Axonemal dynein motors were known to be pre-assembled in the cytoplasm before deployment to cilia (Fowkes and Mitchell, 1998), but the first description of DNAAFs came later, with the identification of KTU (aka DNAAF2)(Omran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Fowkes and Mitchell, 1998.

claim: KTU (aka DNAAF2) was the first described DNAAF.
source: Axonemal dynein motors were known to be pre-assembled in the cytoplasm before deployment to cilia (Fowkes and Mitchell, 1998), but the first description of DNAAFs came later, with the identification of KTU (aka DNAAF2)(Omran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Omran et al., 2008.

claim: DNAAFs are never part of the axoneme.
source: Studies of motile ciliopathy patients have now defined an array of cytoplasmic DNAAFs that are never part of the axoneme, yet when mutated result in loss of axonemal dyneins, and in turn, defective cilia beating (Diggle et al., 2014; Horani et al., 2012; Horani et al., 2013; Kott et al., 2012; Mitchison et al., 2012; Moore et al., 2013; UK10K Rare Group et al., 2017; Paff et al., 2017; UK10K et al., 2013; Zariwala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: When DNAAFs are mutated, they result in loss of axonemal dyneins and defective cilia beating.
source: Studies of motile ciliopathy patients have now defined an array of cytoplasmic DNAAFs that are never part of the axoneme, yet when mutated result in loss of axonemal dyneins, and in turn, defective cilia beating (Diggle et al., 2014; Horani et al., 2012; Horani et al., 2013; Kott et al., 2012; Mitchison et al., 2012; Moore et al., 2013; UK10K Rare Group et al., 2017; Paff et al., 2017; UK10K et al., 2013; Zariwala et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: DNAAFs act in concert with ubiquitous, broadly-acting chaperones of the Heat Shock Protein (Hsp) Family.
source: These specialized DNAAFs are now known to act in concert with ubiquitous, broadly-acting chaperones of the Heat Shock Protein (Hsp) Family (Cho et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mali et al., 2018; UK10K Rare Group et al., 2017; Omran et al., 2008; Paff et al., 2017; UK10K et al., 2013; Yamaguchi et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2013; Zur Lage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Each axoneme contains a series of closely related multiprotein complexes.
source: How DNAAFs organize the assembly of axonemal dyneins is a complex question, as each axoneme contains an series of closely related multiprotein complexes (King, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to King, 2018.

claim: ODAs and IDAs incorporate diverse heavy, intermediate, and light chains encoded by distinct genes.
source: For example, ODAs and IDAs incorporate diverse heavy, intermediate, and light chains encoded by distinct genes; few subunits are shared.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about dynein arm composition.

claim: Few subunits are shared between ODAs and IDAs.
source: For example, ODAs and IDAs incorporate diverse heavy, intermediate, and light chains encoded by distinct genes; few subunits are shared.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about dynein arm composition.

claim: At least eight distinct IDA sub-types and two ODA sub-types have been described.
source: Moreover, at least eight distinct IDA sub-types and two ODA sub-types have been described (Dougherty et al., 2016; Fliegauf et al., 2005; King, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Dougherty et al., 2016; Fliegauf et al., 2005; King, 2018.

claim: Disruption of any single DNAAF has generally been found to impact both ODAs and IDAs.
source: Generally, disruption of any single DNAAF has been found to impact both ODAs and IDAs (Fabczak and Osinka, 2019), but a recent study suggests that distinct DNAAFs may be dedicated for the assembly of specific subsets of dyneins (Yamaguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Fabczak and Osinka, 2019.

claim: Distinct DNAAFs may be dedicated for the assembly of specific subsets of dyneins.
source: Generally, disruption of any single DNAAF has been found to impact both ODAs and IDAs (Fabczak and Osinka, 2019), but a recent study suggests that distinct DNAAFs may be dedicated for the assembly of specific subsets of dyneins (Yamaguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2018.

claim: Distinct DNAAFs may catalyze specific stages of the dynein assembly process.
source: Another recent study has suggested that distinct DNAAFs may catalyze specific stages of the dynein assembly process (Mali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Mali et al., 2018.

claim: DNAAFs and chaperones act together in cytosolic foci.
source: Several studies indicated that the DNAAFs and chaperones act together in cytosolic foci (Diggle et al., 2014; Horani et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017; Mali et al., 2018), and we recently demonstrated that DNAAFs, chaperones, and axonemal dynein subunits are sequestered in specialized membrane-less organelles that we termed DynAPs (Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Diggle et al., 2014; Horani et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017; Mali et al., 2018.

claim: DynAPs are multiciliated cell (MCC)-specific organelles that display hallmarks of biological phase separation.
source: DynAPs are multiciliated cell (MCC)-specific organelles that display hallmarks of biological phase separation, with DNAAFs and chaperones fluxing through rapidly while dynein subunits are stably retained (Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Huizar et al., 2018.

claim: DNAAFs and chaperones flux rapidly through DynAPs while dynein subunits are stably retained.
source: DynAPs are multiciliated cell (MCC)-specific organelles that display hallmarks of biological phase separation, with DNAAFs and chaperones fluxing through rapidly while dynein subunits are stably retained (Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Huizar et al., 2018.

claim: The Hsp co-chaperone Stip1/Hop displays essentially total co-localization with the assembly factor Dnaaf5/Heatr2.
source: We found, for example, that the Hsp co-chaperone Stip1/Hop displayed essentially total co-localization with the assembly factor Dnaaf5/Heatr2 (Figure 1B), while by contrast, the outer dynein arm subunit Dnai2 clearly displayed only partial overlap with Dnaaf5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 1B.

claim: The outer dynein arm subunit Dnai2 displays only partial overlap with Dnaaf5.
source: We found, for example, that the Hsp co-chaperone Stip1/Hop displayed essentially total co-localization with the assembly factor Dnaaf5/Heatr2 (Figure 1B), while by contrast, the outer dynein arm subunit Dnai2 clearly displayed only partial overlap with Dnaaf5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 1C.

claim: Pairwise tests of five distinct DNAAFs and three chaperones revealed consistent, strong co-localization in all combinations.
source: In fact, pairwise tests of five distinct DNAAFs and three chaperones revealed consistent, strong co-localization in all combinations (Figure 1D,E,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 1D, E, G.

claim: Pairwise tests with three different axonemal dynein subunits consistently revealed only partial co-localization.
source: Conversely, pairwise tests with three different axonemal dynein subunits consistently revealed only partial co-localization (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 1F, G.

claim: IDA or ODA subunits occupied distinct, well-demarcated sub-regions within DNAAF- or chaperone-labeled DynAPs.
source: In all cases, IDA or ODA subunits occupied distinct, well-demarcated sub-regions within DNAAF- or chaperone-labeled DynAPs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 1F.

claim: Pearson correlations revealed that differences in co-localization between DNAAFs/chaperones and dynein subunits were statistically significant.
source: Pearson correlations revealed that these differences were statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ODA subunit Dnai2 displayed near-perfect co-localization with two additional ODA sub-units, Dnai1 and Dnal4.
source: For example, the ODA subunit Dnai2 displayed near-perfect co-localization with two additional ODA sub-units, Dnai1 and Dnal4 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 2A, B.

claim: Dnai2 displayed very little colocalization with IDA-f subunit Wdr78 or the IDA-a, c, d subunit Dnali1.
source: By contrast, Dnai2 displayed very little colocalization with IDA-f subunit Wdr78 or the IDA-a, c, d subunit Dnali1 (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Pearson correlations revealed differences in co-localization between ODA and IDA subunits to be highly significant.
source: Again, Pearson correlations revealed these differences to be highly significant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IDAs and ODAs are partitioned into mutually exclusive sub-regions within DynAPs.
source: Strikingly, we found that IDAs and ODAs were partitioned into mutually exclusive sub-regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The IDA-a, c, d subunit Dnali1 and the IDA-f subunit Wdr78 displayed only very little co-localization.
source: For example, the IDA-a, c, d subunit Dnali1 and the IDA-f subunit Wdr78 displayed only very little co-localization (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Wdr78 displayed significantly stronger co-localization with another IDA-f subunit, Tctex1d2.
source: By contrast, Wdr78 displayed significantly stronger co-localized with another IDA-f subunit, Tctex1d2 (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Axonemal dynein subunits are partitioned into functionally distinct sub-regions within DynAPs.
source: Together, these data suggest that axonemal dynein subunits are partitioned into functionally distinct sub-regions; based upon their contents, with ODAs, and at least two sub-classes of IDAs occupying functionally-related restricted spaces within DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the imaging data.

claim: Dnai2 pulldown strongly enriched for known ODA-specific sub-units, including the intermediate chain Dnai1, the heavy chains Dnah9/11, and the light chain Tctex1d1.
source: Dnai2 pulldown strongly enriched for known ODA-specific sub-units, including the intermediate chain Dnai1, the heavy chains Dnah9/11, and the light chain Tctex1d1, among others (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Wdr78 sample was enriched for IDA components, specifically the IDA-f subtype.
source: Conversely, our Wdr78 sample was enriched for IDA components, specifically the IDA-f subtype, as expected (Figure 3C); these included the axonemal dynein heavy chains Dnah2 and Dnah10, as well as several light and intermediate chains (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Dnai2 and Wdr78 showed weaker but significant interaction with a variety of known chaperones and assembly factors, including Ruvbl1/2, Spag1, and Dnaaf1.
source: Finally, we identified weaker but significant interaction of Dnai2 and Wdr78 with a variety of known chaperones and assembly factors, including Ruvbl1/2, Spag1, and Dnaaf1 (Supplementary files 1, 2), consistent with findings that these proteins are enriched in DynAPs and are essential for axonemal dynein assembly (Fabczak and Osinka, 2019; Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: Interaction was observed between Dnai2 and Nme9.
source: For example, we observed interaction between Dnai2 and Nme9 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Figure 3B.

claim: Nme9 is highly similar to the Chlamydomonas ODA light chain LC3.
source: Nme9 is highly similar to the Chlamydomonas ODA light chain LC3 and is present in the axonemes of airway cilia and sperm flagella in mice (Sadek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Sadek et al., 2003.

claim: Nme9 is present in the axonemes of airway cilia and sperm flagella in mice.
source: Nme9 is highly similar to the Chlamydomonas ODA light chain LC3 and is present in the axonemes of airway cilia and sperm flagella in mice (Sadek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Sadek et al., 2003.

claim: Xenopus GFP-Nme9 localized to MCC axonemes.
source: As in mice, Xenopus GFP-Nme9 localized to MCC axonemes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 4A.

claim: GFP-Nme9 was observed in the cytoplasm, where it colocalized with Dnai2 specifically in ODA sub-DynAPs.
source: More importantly, however, we also observed GFP-Nme9 in the cytoplasm, where it colocalized with Dnai2 specifically in ODA sub-DynAPs (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Interaction was observed between Wdr78 and Wdr18.
source: Another notable interaction was that between Wdr78 and Wdr18 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Figure 3C.

claim: Wdr18 has been implicated in the control of ciliary beating, but its mechanism of action is entirely unknown.
source: This result is significant because Wdr18 has been implicated in the control of ciliary beating, but its mechanism of action is entirely unknown (Gao et al., 2011; Silversides et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Gao et al., 2011; Silversides et al., 2012.

claim: GFP-Wdr18 was not present in the axonemes of motile cilia but did localize to DynAPs.
source: Interestingly, GFP-Wdr18 was not present in the axonemes of motile cilia (not shown) but did localize to DynAPs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 4D.

claim: GFP-Wdr18 was strongly enriched in the apical cytoplasm of MCCs, near the basal bodies.
source: Interestingly, GFP-Wdr18 was also strongly enriched in the apical cytoplasm of MCCs, near the basal bodies (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 4E.

claim: Sf3a3 was absent from axonemes but did localize in DynAPs.
source: Similarly, another IDA interactor, Sf3a3 (Figure 3C), was also absent from axonemes (not shown), but did localize in DynAPs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 4F.

claim: Sf3a3 was previously implicated in splicing.
source: This protein was previously implicated in splicing (Krämer et al., 2005), so as expected, we also observed GFP-Sf3a3 in nuclear foci in Xenopus MCCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Krämer et al., 2005.

claim: GFP-Sf3a3 was observed in nuclear foci in Xenopus MCCs.
source: This protein was previously implicated in splicing (Krämer et al., 2005), so as expected, we also observed GFP-Sf3a3 in nuclear foci in Xenopus MCCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most interesting interaction identified was that between Dnai2 and C16orf71.
source: The most interesting interaction we identified in this study was that between Dnai2 and C16orf71 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Figure 3B.

claim: C16orf71 is highly conserved among vertebrates.
source: Though highly conserved among vertebrates, this protein has yet to be the subject of even a single published study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about C16orf71.

claim: C16orf71 has yet to be the subject of even a single published study.
source: Though highly conserved among vertebrates, this protein has yet to be the subject of even a single published study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about C16orf71.

claim: Reciprocal APMS with GFP-tagged Xenopus C16orf71 revealed interaction with Dnai2, Dnai1, Dnah9, Nme9, and Ruvbl1.
source: This analysis revealed interaction of C16orf71 not only with Dnai2, but also other ODA subunits such as Dnai1, Dnah9 and Nme9, as well as Ruvbl1 (Figure 5A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I, Supp. File 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by APMS data in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Xenopus Daap1 expression was enriched in MCCs in the epidermis and the nephrostomes of the pronephros.
source: In situ hybridization revealed that Xenopus Daap1 expression was enriched in MCCs in the epidermis and the nephrostomes of the pronephros (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 5B.

claim: Human DAAP1 protein is present exclusively in tissues with motile cilia.
source: Likewise, examination of data from the Human Protein Atlas (Uhlén et al., 2015) revealed that human DAAP1 protein is present exclusively in tissues with motile cilia (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data from the Human Protein Atlas shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Daap1 is conserved among vertebrates.
source: Interestingly, while Daap1 is conserved among vertebrates, it appears to have followed an interesting evolutionary trajectory.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about Daap1 evolution.

claim: In mammals, including humans, orthologs of Daap1 are composed entirely of a domain of unknown function (DUF4701).
source: In mammals, including humans, orthologs of Daap1 are composed entirely of a domain of unknown function (DUF4701), which phylogenetic analysis suggests is vertebrate-specific (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by domain analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: The DUF4701 domain is vertebrate-specific.
source: In mammals, including humans, orthologs of Daap1 are composed entirely of a domain of unknown function (DUF4701), which phylogenetic analysis suggests is vertebrate-specific (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: The DUF4701 domain sequence is intrinsically disordered.
source: Our analysis of this sequence suggests it is intrinsically disordered (Figure 5E), a feature commonly associated with liquid-like organelles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by disorder prediction analysis in Figure 5E.

claim: Intrinsic disorder is a feature commonly associated with liquid-like organelles.
source: Our analysis of this sequence suggests it is intrinsically disordered (Figure 5E), a feature commonly associated with liquid-like organelles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge about liquid-like organelles.

claim: All non-mammalian vertebrate Daap1 orthologs contain not only the DUF4701 domain, but also a long C-terminal extension harboring an NDK domain similar to those in Nme8 and Nme9.
source: By contrast, all non-mammalian vertebrate Daap1 orthologs contain not only the DUF4701 domain, but also a long C-terminal extension harboring, remarkably, an NDK domain similar to those in Nme8 and Nme9 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by domain analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: No GFP-Daap1 signal was detectable in MCC axonemes.
source: Intriguingly, no signal was detectable in MCC axonemes as marked by Dnai2, and instead, GFP-Daap1 was localized exclusively to foci in the cytoplasm of MCCs (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 6A, B.

claim: GFP-Daap1 was localized exclusively to foci in the cytoplasm of MCCs.
source: Intriguingly, no signal was detectable in MCC axonemes as marked by Dnai2, and instead, GFP-Daap1 was localized exclusively to foci in the cytoplasm of MCCs (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 6A, B.

claim: GFP-Daap1 strongly co-localized with Dnai2.
source: GFP-Daap1 strongly co-localized with Dnai2 (Figure 6B), suggesting that the interaction we identified by APMS occurs in DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 6B.

claim: The interaction between Daap1 and Dnai2 identified by APMS occurs in DynAPs.
source: GFP-Daap1 strongly co-localized with Dnai2 (Figure 6B), suggesting that the interaction we identified by APMS occurs in DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the co-localization data.

claim: Daap1 displayed a partial co-localization with Dnaaf2 similar to that observed in the cytoplasm for other ODA subunits.
source: Indeed, Daap1 displayed a partial co-localization with Dnaaf2 similar to that observed in the cytoplasm for other ODA subunits (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 6C.

claim: Daap1 displayed little or no overlap with GFP-Wdr78.
source: Finally, Daap1 displayed little or no overlap with GFP-Wdr78 (Figure 6D), suggesting that it localized specifically in ODA sub-DynAPs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 6D.

claim: Daap1 localized specifically in ODA sub-DynAPs.
source: Finally, Daap1 displayed little or no overlap with GFP-Wdr78 (Figure 6D), suggesting that it localized specifically in ODA sub-DynAPs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the co-localization data.

claim: Human DAAP1 lacks the C-terminal NDK domain present in the Xenopus ortholog.
source: Because human DAAP1 lacks the C-terminal NDK domain present in the Xenopus ortholog (Figure 5D), we were curious to know if the human ortholog also localizes to DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by domain analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: Human DAAP1 was not detectable in the axonemes of human MCCs.
source: As observed in Xenopus, DAAP1 was not detectable in the axonemes of human MCCs (Figure 7A, brackets), and cytoplasmic staining for DAAP1 was strongly enriched in DynAPs, as indicated by co-labeling for the ODA subunit DNAI1 (Figure 7A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7A.

claim: Cytoplasmic staining for human DAAP1 was strongly enriched in DynAPs.
source: As observed in Xenopus, DAAP1 was not detectable in the axonemes of human MCCs (Figure 7A, brackets), and cytoplasmic staining for DAAP1 was strongly enriched in DynAPs, as indicated by co-labeling for the ODA subunit DNAI1 (Figure 7A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7A.

claim: GFP-Daap1-Nterm also localized to ODA sub-DynAPs in Xenopus MCCs.
source: We found that GFP-Daap1-Nterm also localized to ODA sub-DynAPs in Xenopus MCCs (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 7C–E.

claim: Both Xenopus and human DAAP1 are DynAP-specific cytoplasmic proteins.
source: Thus, despite their divergent evolutionary trajectories, both Xenopus and human DAAP1 are DynAP-specific cytoplasmic proteins, and the N-terminal DUF4701 domain is sufficient to direct localization to ODA sub-DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the localization data.

claim: The N-terminal DUF4701 domain is sufficient to direct localization to ODA sub-DynAPs.
source: Thus, despite their divergent evolutionary trajectories, both Xenopus and human DAAP1 are DynAP-specific cytoplasmic proteins, and the N-terminal DUF4701 domain is sufficient to direct localization to ODA sub-DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the localization data of the N-terminal construct.

claim: DNAAFs and broadly-acting chaperones flux rapidly through DynAPs.
source: DynAPs are liquid-like organelles, and we previously found using FRAP that both the DNAAFs and broadly-acting chaperones flux rapidly through these organelles, while both ODA and IDA subunits are stably retained (Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Huizar et al., 2018.

claim: Both ODA and IDA subunits are stably retained in DynAPs.
source: DynAPs are liquid-like organelles, and we previously found using FRAP that both the DNAAFs and broadly-acting chaperones flux rapidly through these organelles, while both ODA and IDA subunits are stably retained (Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Huizar et al., 2018.

claim: FRAP revealed that Xenopus Daap1 was retained in DynAPs in a manner that was similar, but not identical, to dynein subunit Dnai2.
source: To our surprise, however, FRAP revealed instead that Xenopus Daap1 was retained in DynAPs in a manner that was similar, but not identical, to dynein subunit Dnai2 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 8.

claim: Daap1 displayed a somewhat slower initial recovery than Dnai2, but the signal continued to slowly recover for at least 60 s.
source: Specifically, Daap1 displayed a somewhat slower initial recovery, but rather than plateauing at around 20 s, the signal continued to slowly recover for at least 60 s (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 8B.

claim: Daap1-Nterm displayed essentially identical FRAP kinetics to full-length Daap1.
source: In FRAP assays, Daap1-Nterm displayed essentially identical kinetics to full-length Daap1 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 8B.

claim: The DUF4701 domain is sufficient to drive the retention of Daap1 in ODA sub-DynAPs.
source: This result is consistent with the localization data above and strongly suggests that the DUF4701 domain is sufficient to drive the retention of Daap1 in ODA sub-DynAPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the FRAP data.

claim: Daap1-KD had no impact on ciliogenesis itself.
source: Consistent with its interaction specifically with ciliary beating machinery, Daap1-KD had no impact on ciliogenesis itself, and well-defined ciliary tufts were observed in all morphants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from knockdown experiments.

claim: Daap1-KD elicited severe loss of ODAs from MCC axonemes.
source: However, Daap1-KD elicited severe loss of ODAs from MCC axonemes (Figure 9A,B, D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 9A, B, D, E.

claim: Both the intermediate chain Dnai2 and the light chain Dnal1 were severely reduced after Daap1-KD, with only small domains of the proximal axoneme labeled by either marker.
source: Both the intermediate chain Dnai2, as well as the light chain Dnal1 were severely reduced, with only small domains of the proximal axoneme labeled by either marker following knockdown (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 9A, B.

claim: The ODA depletion phenotype was also observed using a second MO targeting a distinct splice site.
source: Importantly, this phenotype was also observed using a second MO targeting a distinct splice site, suggesting that this phenotype is a specific effect of Daap1 depletion. (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: While both ODA proteins were depleted along the entire length of the axoneme after Daap1 loss, the IDA-a, c, d protein Dnali1 and the IDA-f protein Wdr78 displayed more subtle defects.
source: While both ODA proteins were depleted along the entire length of the axoneme, the IDA-a, c, d protein Dnali1 and the IDA-f protein Wdr78 displayed more subtle defects (Figure 9G,H,J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 9G, H, J, K.

claim: Dnali1 displayed a mild reduction along the entire axoneme after Daap1 loss.
source: Dnali1 displayed a mild reduction along the entire axoneme (Figure 9I), while Wdr78 displayed an even mild disruption that was largely restricted to the distal axoneme (Figure 9L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 9I.

claim: Wdr78 displayed a mild disruption that was largely restricted to the distal axoneme after Daap1 loss.
source: Dnali1 displayed a mild reduction along the entire axoneme (Figure 9I), while Wdr78 displayed an even mild disruption that was largely restricted to the distal axoneme (Figure 9L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 9L.

claim: Loss of Daap1 had a significantly greater impact on ODA compared to IDAs.
source: Overall, comparisons of subunit intensities demonstrated that loss of Daap1 had a significantly greater impact on ODA compared to IDAs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the intensity analysis.

claim: Direct comparison of Wdr78 and Dnai1 co-expressed in the same axonemes demonstrated a profoundly more substantial loss of ODAs than IDAs after Daap1 depletion.
source: This analysis clearly demonstrated a profoundly more substantial loss of ODAs than IDAs after Daap1 depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 9M–P.

claim: Daap1 is a DynAP-specific protein that interacts with ODA subunits and is essential for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes.
source: Thus, Daap1 is a DynAP-specific protein that interacts with ODA subunits and is essential for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes and further suggests a complex interplay of ODAs and IDAs is required to establish the final patterning of motors that drive ciliary beating.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the localization and functional data.

claim: A complex interplay of ODAs and IDAs is required to establish the final patterning of motors that drive ciliary beating.
source: Thus, Daap1 is a DynAP-specific protein that interacts with ODA subunits and is essential for the deployment of ODAs to axonemes and further suggests a complex interplay of ODAs and IDAs is required to establish the final patterning of motors that drive ciliary beating.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the functional data.

claim: DynAPs have been observed in human, mouse, Xenopus and zebrafish.
source: DynAPs have now been observed in human, mouse, Xenopus and zebrafish, so it is clear that these organelles represent a conserved element of MCCs (Diggle et al., 2014; Horani et al., 2018; Huizar et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with multiple citations.

claim: DynAPs represent a conserved element of MCCs.
source: DynAPs have now been observed in human, mouse, Xenopus and zebrafish, so it is clear that these organelles represent a conserved element of MCCs (Diggle et al., 2014; Horani et al., 2018; Huizar et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from observations across species.

claim: Genetic loss of DynAP-localized DNAAFs consistently results in a failure of dynein arm assembly, failure of dynein deployment to axonemes, and defective ciliary beating.
source: Genetic evidence suggests that DynAPs are factories for axonemal dynein assembly, as genetic loss of DynAP-localized DNAAFs consistently results in a failure of dynein arm assembly, failure of dynein deployment to axonemes, and defective ciliary beating (Fabczak and Osinka, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Fabczak and Osinka, 2019.

claim: Identification of Daap1 as a protein enriched in DynAPs and specifically required for deployment of axonemal dyneins to cilia adds weight to the argument that DynAPs perform a critical assembly or deployment function.
source: Our identification of Daap1 as yet another protein that is enriched in DynAPs and is specifically required for deployment of axonemal dyneins to cilia adds weight to the argument that DynAPs perform a critical assembly or deployment function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: DynAPs are structurally partitioned.
source: Regardless, our data clearly demonstrate that DynAPs are structurally partitioned, as are many other liquid-like organelles (e.g. Feric et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Schmidt and Rohatgi, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the imaging data, with citations to other liquid-like organelles.

claim: Many other liquid-like organelles are structurally partitioned.
source: Regardless, our data clearly demonstrate that DynAPs are structurally partitioned, as are many other liquid-like organelles (e.g. Feric et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Schmidt and Rohatgi, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Feric et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Schmidt and Rohatgi, 2016.

claim: The observation that Daap1 is restricted to ODA sub-DynAPs and that its loss results predominantly in ODA defects argues that sub-DynAPs reflect a functional sub-compartmentalization.
source: Moreover, our observation that Daap1 is restricted to ODA sub-DynAPs (Figures 6 and 7) and that its loss results predominantly in ODA defects (Figure 9) argues that sub-DynAPs reflect a functional sub-compartmentalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the localization and functional data.

claim: There is no evidence of physical compartmentalization of any of the tested DNAAFs and chaperones.
source: Conversely, though it has been suggested that DNAAFs and chaperones act in a relay system to catalyze iterative steps of ODA and IDA assembly (Mali et al., 2018), we found no evidence of physical compartmentalization of any of the tested DNAAFs and chaperones (Figure 1), suggesting that partitioned localization of those factors is not strictly required.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Partitioned localization of DNAAFs and chaperones is not strictly required for their function.
source: Conversely, though it has been suggested that DNAAFs and chaperones act in a relay system to catalyze iterative steps of ODA and IDA assembly (Mali et al., 2018), we found no evidence of physical compartmentalization of any of the tested DNAAFs and chaperones (Figure 1), suggesting that partitioned localization of those factors is not strictly required.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the lack of compartmentalization observed.

claim: Ktu has been shown to specifically impact assembly of ODAs and IDA-c.
source: Consistent with this idea, though Ktu has been shown to specifically impact assembly of ODAs and IDA-c (Yamaguchi et al., 2018), we found no restriction of Ktu localization within DynAPs (Figure 1 and see Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2018.

claim: There is no restriction of Ktu localization within DynAPs.
source: Consistent with this idea, though Ktu has been shown to specifically impact assembly of ODAs and IDA-c (Yamaguchi et al., 2018), we found no restriction of Ktu localization within DynAPs (Figure 1 and see Huizar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by imaging data in Figure 1 and citation to Huizar et al., 2018.
